{{Short description|Kind of proposition in mathematics}}
{{other uses}}
In [[set theory]], a branch of [[mathematics]], a '''reflection principle''' says that it is possible to find sets that, with respect to any given property, resemble the [[class (set theory)|class]] of all sets. There are several different forms of the reflection principle depending on exactly what is meant by "resemble". Weak forms of the reflection principle are theorems of [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory]] (<math>\mathsf{ZF}</math>) due to {{harvtxt|Montague|1961}}, while stronger forms can be new and very powerful axioms for set theory.

The name "reflection principle" comes from the fact that properties of the universe of all sets are "reflected" down to a smaller set.

==Motivation==
A naive version of the reflection principle states that "for any property of the universe of all sets we can find a set with the same property". This leads to an immediate contradiction: the universe of all sets contains all sets, but there is no set with the property that it contains all sets. To get useful (and non-contradictory) reflection principles we need to be more careful about what we mean by "property" and what properties we allow.

Reflection principles are associated with attempts to formulate the idea that no one notion, idea, or statement can capture our whole view of [[von Neumann universe|the universe of sets]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Welch |first=Philip D. |date=12 November 2019 |chapter=Proving Theorems from Reflection |title=Reflections on the Foundations of Mathematics |series=Synthese Library |volume=407 |chapter-url=https://research-information.bris.ac.uk/en/publications/5f593268-df18-4dcc-801a-bb9e302015a1 |publisher=Springer, Cham |pages=79–97 |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-15655-8_4 |isbn=978-3-030-15655-8|s2cid=192577454 }}</ref> [[Kurt Gödel]] described it as follows:<ref name="Wang">{{cite book |last=Wang |first=Hao |author-link=Hao Wang (academic) |date=March 25, 2016 |title= A Logical Journey: From Gödel to Philosophy |url=https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262529167/a-logical-journey/ |publisher=Bradford Books |pages=280–285 |isbn=978-0262529167}}</ref>

{{Blockquote |text=The universe of all sets is structurally indefinable. One possible way to make this statement precise is the following: The universe of sets cannot be uniquely characterized (i.e., distinguished from all its initial segments) by any internal structural property of the membership relation in it which is expressible in any logic of finite or [[transfinite number|transfinite]] type, including [[infinitary logics]] of any [[cardinal number]]. This principle may be considered a generalization of the [[closure (mathematics)|closure]] principle.
|source=8.7.3, p. 280}}

{{Blockquote |text=All the principles for setting up the [[axiomatic set theory|axioms of set theory]] should be reducible to [[Wilhelm Ackermann|Ackermann]]'s principle: The [[Absolute infinite|Absolute]] is unknowable. The strength of this principle increases as we get stronger and stronger systems of set theory. The other principles are only heuristic principles. Hence, the central principle is the reflection principle, which presumably will be understood better as our experience increases. Meanwhile, it helps to separate out more specific principles which either give some additional information or are not yet seen clearly to be derivable from the reflection principle as we understand it now.
|source=8.7.9, p. 283}}

{{Blockquote |text=Generally I believe that, in the last analysis, every [[axiom of infinity]] should be derivable from the (extremely plausible) principle that [[Von Neumann universe|V]] is indefinable, where definability is to be taken in [a] more and more generalized and idealized sense.
|source=8.7.16, p. 285}}

[[Georg Cantor]] expressed similar views on [[absolute infinity]]: All cardinality properties are satisfied in this number, in which held by a smaller cardinal.

To find non-contradictory reflection principles we might argue informally as follows. Suppose that we have some collection ''A'' of methods for forming sets (for example, taking [[powerset]]s, [[subset]]s, the [[axiom of replacement]], and so on). We can imagine taking all sets obtained by repeatedly applying all these methods, and form these sets into a class ''X'', which can be thought of as a [[model (logic)|model]] of some set theory. But in light of this view, V is not exhaustible by a handful of operations, otherwise it would be easily describable from below, this principle is known as inexhaustibility (of V).<ref name="Maddy88">P. Maddy, "[https://www.cs.umd.edu/~gasarch/BLOGPAPERS/belaxioms1.pdf Believing the Axioms. I]", pp.501–503. [[Journal of Symbolic Logic]] vol. 53, no. 2 (1988).</ref> As a result, V is larger than ''X''. Applying the methods in ''A'' to the set ''X'' itself would also result in a collection smaller than V, as V is not exhaustible from the image of ''X'' under the operations in ''A''. Then we can introduce the following new principle for forming sets: "the collection of all sets obtained from some set by repeatedly applying all methods in the collection ''A'' is also a set". After adding this principle to ''A'', V is still not exhaustible by the operations in this new ''A''. This process may be repeated further and further, adding more and more operations to the set ''A'' and obtaining larger and larger models ''X''. Each ''X'' resembles V in the sense that it shares the property with V of being closed under the operations in ''A''.

We can use this informal argument in two ways. We can try to formalize it in (say) <math>\mathsf{ZF}</math>; by doing this we obtain some theorems of <math>\mathsf{ZF}</math>, called reflection theorems. Alternatively we can use this argument to motivate introducing new axioms for set theory, such as some [[List of large cardinal properties|axioms asserting existence of large cardinals]].<ref name="Maddy88" />

==In ZFC==
In trying to formalize the argument for the reflection principle of the previous section in <math>\mathsf{ZF}</math>, it turns out to be necessary to add some conditions about the collection of properties ''A'' (for example, ''A'' might be finite). Doing this produces several closely related "reflection theorems" all of which state that we can find a set that is almost a model of [[ZFC]]. In contrast to stronger reflection principles, these are provable in <math>\mathsf{ZFC}</math>.

One of the most common reflection principles for <math>\mathsf{ZFC}</math> is a theorem schema that can be described as follows: for any formula <math>\phi(x_1,\ldots,x_n)</math> with parameters, if <math>\phi(x_1,\ldots,x_n)</math> is true (in the set-theoretic universe <math>V</math>), then there is a level <math>V_\alpha</math> of the [[cumulative hierarchy]] such that <math>V_\alpha\vDash\phi(x_1,\ldots,x_n)</math>. This is known as the Lévy–Montague reflection principle,<ref>{{cite journal|arxiv=1708.06669 |doi=10.1007/s11225-019-09860-7 |title=Inner-Model Reflection Principles |date=2020 |last1=Barton |first1=Neil |last2=Caicedo |first2=Andrés Eduardo |last3=Fuchs |first3=Gunter |last4=Hamkins |first4=Joel David |author4link = Joel David Hamkins|last5=Reitz |first5=Jonas |last6=Schindler |first6=Ralf |journal=[[Studia Logica]] |volume=108 |issue=3 |pages=573–595 |s2cid=255073980 }}</ref> or the Lévy reflection principle,<ref>S. D. Friedman, [http://www.logic.univie.ac.at/~sdf/papers/chiemsee.pdf Evidence for Set-Theoretic Truth and the Hyperuniverse Programme] (2016), p.15. Accessed 28 March 2023.</ref> principally investigated in {{harvtxt|Lévy|1960}} and {{harvtxt|Montague|1961}}.<ref>A. Kanamori, ''The Higher Infinite'', p.58. Springer Monographs in Mathematics (2003). ISBN 978-3-540-88866-6.</ref> Another version of this reflection principle says that for any '''finite''' number of formulas of <math>\mathsf{ZFC}</math> we can find a set <math>V_\alpha</math> in the cumulative hierarchy such that all the formulas in the set are [[absoluteness (mathematical logic)|absolute]] for <math>V_\alpha</math> (which means very roughly that they hold in <math>V_\alpha</math> if and only if they hold in the universe of all sets). So this says that the set <math>V_\alpha</math> resembles the universe of all sets, at least as far as the given finite number of formulas is concerned.

Another reflection principle for <math>\mathsf{ZFC}</math> is a theorem schema that can be described as follows:<ref>{{cite web |url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/000F |title=Section 3.8 (000F): Reflection principle |author-link=The Stacks Project |date=2022 |website=The Stacks Project |access-date=7 September 2022}}</ref><ref>T. Jech, 'Set Theory: The Third Millennium Edition, revised and expanded', pp.168–170. Springer Monographs in Mathematics (2006). ISBN 3-540-44085-2</ref> Let <math>\phi</math> be a formula with at most [[free variables]] <math>x_1, \ldots, x_n</math>. Then <math>\mathsf{ZFC}</math> proves that
:<math>(\forall N) (\exists M {\supseteq} N) (\forall x_1, \ldots, x_n {\in} M) (\phi(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \leftrightarrow \phi^M)</math>
where <math>\phi^M</math> denotes the ''relativization'' of <math>\phi</math> to <math>M</math> (that is, replacing all [[quantifier (logic)|quantifiers]] appearing in <math>\phi</math> of the form <math>\forall x</math> and <math>\exists x</math> by <math>\forall x {\in} M</math> and <math>\exists x {\in} M</math>, respectively).

Another form of the reflection principle in <math>\mathsf{ZFC}</math> says that for any '''finite''' set of axioms of <math>\mathsf{ZFC}</math> we can find a countable [[set model|transitive model]] satisfying these axioms. (In particular this proves that, unless [[consistent|inconsistent]], <math>\mathsf{ZFC}</math> is not finitely axiomatizable because if it were it would prove the existence of a model of itself, and hence prove its own consistency, contradicting [[Gödel's second incompleteness theorem]].) This version of the reflection theorem is closely related to the [[Löwenheim–Skolem theorem]].

If <math>\kappa</math> is a [[inaccessible cardinal|strong inaccessible cardinal]], then there is a [[club set|closed unbounded subset]] <math>C</math> of <math>\kappa</math>, such that for every <math>\alpha\in C</math>, <math>V_\alpha</math> is an [[elementary substructure]] of <math>V_\kappa</math>.{{sfn|Jech|2002|p=171|loc=exercise 12.12}}

==As new axioms==

===Large cardinals===

Reflection principles are connected to and can be used to motivate large cardinal axioms. Reinhardt gives the following examples, using Cantor's informal notion of [[Absolute infinite|absolute infinity]] in place of the universe of sets:<ref name="ReinhardtReflection">{{citation|mr=0401475
|last=Reinhardt|first= W. N.
|chapter=Remarks on reflection principles, large cardinals, and elementary embeddings. |title=Axiomatic set theory |series=Proc. Sympos. Pure Math.|volume= XIII, Part II|pages= 189–205|publisher= Amer. Math. Soc.|publication-place= Providence, R. I.|year= 1974|contribution-url=https://canvas.eee.uci.edu/courses/8140/files/2966398/download?verifier=2cFyXQWmyjg7qKTxIbBasupeSVEkZQZJaE1yGkWz&download_frd=1}}</ref>

: It may be helpful to give some informal arguments illustrating the use of reflection principles.
: The simplest is perhaps: the universe of sets is inaccessible (i.e., satisfies the replacement axiom), ''therefore'' there is an inaccessible cardinal. This can be elaborated somewhat, as follows. Let <math>\theta_\nu</math> enumerate the inaccessible cardinals. By the same sort of reasoning, <math>\theta_\nu</math> is not bounded; the Cantor absolute <math>\Omega</math> (all ordinals) is an inaccessible above any proposed bound <math>\beta</math>, ''therefore'' there is an inaccessible cardinal above <math>\beta</math>. Clearly, then, there are <math>\Omega</math> inaccessibles above below <math>\Omega</math>; ''therefore'' there is an inaccessible <math>\kappa</math> such that there are <math>\kappa</math> inaccessibles below it (i.e., <math>\kappa=\theta_\kappa</math>).

===Bernays class theory===

[[Paul Bernays]] used a reflection principle as an axiom for one version of set theory (not [[Von Neumann–Bernays–Gödel set theory]], which is a weaker theory). His reflection principle stated roughly that if <math>A</math> is a class with some property, then one can find a transitive set <math>u</math> such that <math>A\cap u</math> has the same property when considered as a subset of the "universe" <math>u</math>. This is quite a powerful axiom and implies the existence of several of the smaller [[large cardinal]]s, such as [[inaccessible cardinal]]s. (Roughly speaking, the class of all [[ordinal number|ordinals]] in <math>\mathsf{ZFC}</math> is an inaccessible cardinal apart from the fact that it is not a set, and the reflection principle can then be used to show that there is a set that has the same property, in other words that is an inaccessible cardinal.) Unfortunately, this cannot be axiomatized directly in <math>\mathsf{ZFC}</math>, and a class theory like [[Morse–Kelley set theory]] normally has to be used. The consistency of Bernays's reflection principle is implied by the existence of an [[Erdős cardinal|ω-Erdős cardinal]].

More precisely, the axioms of Bernays' class theory are:<ref name="Marshall">{{cite journal |last1=Marshall R. |first1=M. Victoria |date=1989 |title=Higher order reflection principles |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-symbolic-logic/article/abs/higher-order-reflection-principles/1332BC3404FAB6187AF58990D591538B |journal=The Journal of Symbolic Logic |volume=54 |issue=2 |pages=474–489 |doi=10.2307/2274862 |jstor=2274862 |s2cid=250351126 |access-date=9 September 2022|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
# [[axiom of extensionality|extensionality]]
# class [[axiom of specification|specification]]: for any formula <math>\phi</math> without <math>a</math> free, <math>\exists a \forall b (b \in a \leftrightarrow \phi \land b \text{ is a set})</math>
# [[subsets]]: <math>b \subseteq a \land a \text{ is a set} \to b \text{ is a set}</math>
# reflection: for any formula <math>\phi</math>, <math>\phi(A) \to \exists u (u \text{ is a transitive set} \land \phi^{\mathcal{P} u}(A \cap u))</math>
# [[axiom of foundation|foundation]]
# [[axiom of choice|choice]]
where <math>\mathcal{P}</math> denotes the [[powerset]].

According to [[Akihiro Kanamori]],<ref>{{cite journal |last=Kanamori |first=Akihiro |author-link=Akihiro Kanamori |date=March 2009 |title=Bernays and Set Theory |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/25470304 |journal=[[The Bulletin of Symbolic Logic]] |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=43–69 |doi=10.2178/bsl/1231081769|jstor=25470304 |s2cid=15567244 | access-date=9 September 2022}}</ref>{{rp|62}} in a 1961 paper, Bernays considered the reflection schema
:<math>\phi \to \exists x (\text{transitive}(x) \land \phi^x)</math>
for any formula <math>\phi</math> without <math>x</math> free, where <math>\text{transitive}(x)</math> asserts that <math>x</math> is [[transitive set|transitive]]. Starting with the observation that set parameters <math>a_1,\ldots,a_n</math> can appear in <math>\phi</math> and <math>x</math> can be required to contain them by introducing clauses <math>\exists y (a_i \in y)</math> into <math>\phi</math>, Bernays just with this schema established [[axiom of pairing|pairing]], [[axiom of union|union]], [[axiom of infinity|infinity]], and [[axiom of replacement|replacement]], in effect achieving a remarkably economical presentation of <math>\mathsf{ZF}</math>.

===Others===
Some formulations of [[Ackermann set theory]] use a reflection principle. Ackermann's axiom states that, for any formula <math>\phi</math> not mentioning <math>V</math>,<ref name="Wang"/>{{rp|282}}
:<math>a \in V \land b \in V \to \forall x (\phi \to x \in V) \to \exists u {\in} V \forall x (x \in u \leftrightarrow \phi)</math>

[[Peter Koellner]] showed that a general class of reflection principles deemed "intrinsically justified" are either [[inconsistent]] or weak, in that they are consistent relative to the [[Erdös cardinal]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Koellner |first1=Peter |date=February 2009 |title=On reflection principles |journal=[[Annals of Pure and Applied Logic]] |volume=157 |issue=2 |pages=206–219 |doi=10.1016/j.apal.2008.09.007 |doi-access= }}</ref> However, there are more powerful reflection principles, which are closely related to the various large cardinal axioms. For almost every known large cardinal axiom there is a known reflection principle that implies it, and conversely all but the most powerful known reflection principles are implied by known large cardinal axioms.<ref name="Marshall"/> An example of this is the [[wholeness axiom]],<ref>{{cite journal|title=The Wholeness Axiom and Laver Sequences|authorlink=Paul Corazza|first=Paul|last= Corazza|journal=Annals of Pure and Applied Logic |volume= 105|year=2000|issue=1–3 |pages= 157–260|doi=10.1016/s0168-0072(99)00052-4|doi-access=free}}
</ref> which implies the existence of [[huge cardinal|super-''n''-huge cardinal]]s for all finite ''n'' and its consistency is implied by an I3 [[rank-into-rank|rank-into-rank cardinal]].

Add an axiom saying that ''Ord'' is a [[Mahlo cardinal]] &mdash; for every closed unbounded class of ordinals ''C'' (definable by a formula with parameters), there is a [[regular ordinal]] in ''C''. This allows one to derive the existence of strong [[inaccessible cardinal]]s and much more over any ordinal.

==For arithmetic==

Reflection principles may be considered for theories of arithmetic, which are generally much weaker than <math>\mathsf{ZFC}</math>.

===Soundness===

Let <math>\mathsf{PA}</math> denote [[Peano_axioms#Peano_arithmetic_as_first-order_theory|Peano arithmetic]], and <math>\mathsf{PA}_k</math> denote the [[True arithmetic|set of true sentences in the language of PA]] that are <math>\Sigma_k</math> in the [[arithmetical hierarchy]]. [[Andrzej Mostowski|Mostowski]]'s reflection theorem states that for each natural number <math>k</math>, <math>\mathsf{PA}</math> proves the consistency of <math>\mathsf{PA}_k</math>. As each set <math>\mathsf{PA}_k</math> is <math>\Sigma_k</math>-definable, this must be expressed as a theorem schema.<ref>{{cite arXiv|eprint=1801.04599 |author1=Joel David Hamkins |title=The modal logic of arithmetic potentialism and the universal algorithm |date=2018 |class=math.LO }}</ref><sup>p. 4</sup> These soundness principles are sometimes referred to as [[Syntax (logic)|syntactic]] reflection principles, in contrast to the satisfaction-based varieties mentioned above, which are called [[Semantics (logic)|semantic]] reflection principles.<ref>{{cite arXiv|eprint=2103.12147 |last1=Pakhomov |first1=Fedor |last2=Walsh |first2=James |title=Reducing $ω$-model reflection to iterated syntactic reflection |date=2021 |class=math.LO }}</ref><sup>p. 1</sup>

The local reflection principle <math>Rfn(T)</math> for a theory <math>T</math> is the schema that for each sentence <math>\phi</math> of the language of <math>T</math>, <math>\mathrm{Prov}_T(\phi)\implies\phi</math>. When <math>Rfn_\Gamma(T)</math> denotes the restricted version of the principle only considering those <math>\phi</math> in a class of formulas <math>\Gamma</math>, we have that <math>\mathrm{Con}(T)</math> and <math>Rfn_{\Pi^0_1}(T)</math> are equivalent over <math>T</math>.<ref name="Tsuboi82">A. Tsuboi, "On reflection principles". Tsukuba J. Math, vol. 6, no. 2 (1982).</ref><sup>p. 205</sup>

The uniform reflection principle <math>RFN(T)</math> for a theory <math>T</math> is the schema that for each natural number <math>n</math>, <math>\forall(\ulcorner\phi\urcorner\in\Sigma^0_n\cup\Pi^0_n)\forall(y_0,\ldots,y_m\in\mathbb N)(\mathrm{Pr}_T(\ulcorner\phi(y_0,\ldots,y_n)^*\urcorner\implies\mathrm{Tr}_n(\ulcorner\phi(y_0,\ldots,y_n)^*\urcorner))</math>, where <math>\Sigma^0_n\cup\Pi^0_n</math> is the union of the sets of [[Gödel numbering|Gödel-numbers]] of <math>\Sigma^0_n</math> and <math>\Pi^0_n</math> formulas, and <math>\phi(y_0,\ldots,y_n)^*</math> is <math>\phi</math> with its free variables <math>y_0,\ldots,y_m</math> replaced with numerals <math>\underbrace{S\ldots S}_{y_0}0</math>, etc. in the language of Peano arithmetic, and <math>\mathrm{Tr}_n</math> is the partial [[truth predicate]] for <math>\Sigma^0_n\cup\Pi^0_n</math> formulas.<ref name="Tsuboi82" /><sup>p. 205</sup>

===Model reflection===

For <math>k\geq 1</math>, a [[Beta-model|<math>\beta_k</math>-model]] is a model  that has the correct truth values of <math>\Pi^1_k</math> statements, where <math>\Pi^1_k</math> is at the <math>(k+1)</math>th level of the [[analytical hierarchy]]. A countable <math>\beta_k</math>-model of a subsystem of [[second-order arithmetic]] consists of a countable set of sets of natural numbers, which may itself be encoded as a subset of <math>\mathbb N</math>. The theory <math>\Pi^1_1\text{-}\mathsf{CA}_0</math> proves the existence of a <math>\beta_1</math>-model, also known as a <math>\beta</math>-model.<ref name="Simpson2009">[[Steve Simpson (mathematician)|S. G. Simpson]], ''Subsystems of Second Order Arithmetic'' (2009)</ref><sup>Theorem VII.2.16</sup>

The <math>\beta_k</math>-model reflection principle for <math>\Sigma^1_n</math> formulas states that for any <math>\Sigma^1_n</math> formula <math>\theta(X)</math> with <math>X</math> as its only free set variable, for all <math>X\subseteq\mathbb N</math>, if <math>\theta(X)</math> holds, then there is a countable coded <math>\beta_k</math>-model <math>M</math> where <math>X\in M</math> such that <math>M\vDash\theta(X)</math>. An extension <math>\Sigma^1_k\text{-}\mathsf{DC}_0</math> of <math>\mathsf{ACA}_0</math> by a schema of dependent choice is axiomatized. For any <math>0\leq k</math>, the system <math>\Sigma^1_{k+2}\text{-}\mathsf{DC}_0</math> is equivalent to <math>\beta_{k+1}</math>-reflection for <math>\Sigma^1_{k+4}</math> formulas.<ref name="Simpson2009" /><sup>Theorem VII.7.6</sup>

<math>\beta</math>-model reflection has connections to set-theoretic reflection, for example over the weak set theory [[Kripke-Platek set theory|KP]], adding the schema of reflection of <math>\Pi_n</math>-formulas to transitive sets (<math>\phi\implies\exists z(\textrm{transitive}(z)\land\phi^z)</math> for all <math>\Pi_n</math> formulas <math>\phi</math>) yields the same <math>\Pi^1_4</math>-consequeneces as <math>\mathsf{ACA+BI}</math> plus a schema of <math>\beta</math>-model reflection for <math>\Pi^1_{n+1}</math> formulas.<ref>M. Rathjen, "[https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0168007294900744 Proof Theory of Reflection]". Annals of Pure and Applied Logic, vol. 68, issue 2 (1994), pp.181–224.</ref>
